metadata.title: Finer-Resolution Long-Term Plant Functional Types-specific Leaf Area Index at 500-m Resolution for Earth System Modeling – Year 2015
metadata.description:
This dataset provides a global monthly plant functional type–specific leaf area index (PFT LAI) product at 500 m spatial resolution for the period 1985–2020. The dataset was developed by combining the PFT dataset with reprocessed MODIS Collection 6.1 LAI and GIMMS LAI4g products, using a remote-sensing-derived phenology scheme rather than conventional empirical approaches. By directly constraining phenological dynamics with satellite observations, the PFT LAI dataset captures realistic seasonal variations across different vegetation types. It enables detailed analysis of vegetation dynamics and land surface processes and supports fine-scale simulations and long-term assessments of land use and land cover change impacts.

The dataset is provided in NetCDF format using a 5° × 5° spatial tiling scheme, with files corresponding to each 30° × 30° region packaged into a single tar archive, named as RG_{latN}_{lonW}_{latS}_{lonE}.LSAI500m.{YEAR}.tar. Due to the large volume of the full long-term dataset, this deposition provides data for the year 2015 only. Data for 2005 is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18113489, and data for other years can be provided upon request. The corresponding PFT dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18139027.

metadata.title: Global Snow-free Leaf Area Index Dataset for Earth System Modeling – Year 2015
metadata.description:
The snow-free Leaf Area Index (LAI) dataset is a global monthly LAI product developed for land surface and earth system modeling. It covers the period from 1985 to 2020 at 500 m spatial resolution and aims to constrain the underestimation of LAI in snow-covered regions caused by snow contamination.

The dataset was generated by integrating reprocessed MODIS Collection 6.1 LAI and GIMMS LAI4g products with plant functional type (PFT) information. Snow-affected areas were identified using satellite-based observations, and LAI was corrected at the PFT level using leaf lifespan constraints derived from the TRY plant trait database. The resulting snow-free LAI better represents the phenology of evergreen vegetation and is intended to support studies of vegetation–snow interactions, land surface processes, and earth system modeling.

The dataset is provided in NetCDF format using a 5° × 5° spatial tiling scheme, with files corresponding to each 30° × 30° region packaged into a single tar archive, named as RG_{latN}_{lonW}_{latS}_{lonE}.LSAI500m.{YEAR}.tar. Due to the large volume of the full long-term dataset, this deposition provides data for the year 2015 only. Data for 2005 are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18098037, and data for other years can be provided upon request. The corresponding PFT dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18139027.

metadata.title: Global Snow-free Leaf Area Index Dataset for Earth System Modeling – Year 1998
metadata.description:
The snow-free Leaf Area Index (LAI) dataset is a global monthly LAI product developed for land surface and earth system modeling. It covers the period from 1985 to 2020 at 500 m spatial resolution and aims to constrain the underestimation of LAI in snow-covered regions caused by snow contamination.

The dataset was generated by integrating reprocessed MODIS Collection 6.1 LAI and GIMMS LAI4g products with plant functional type (PFT) information. Snow-affected areas were identified using satellite-based observations, and LAI was corrected at the PFT level using leaf lifespan constraints derived from the TRY plant trait database. The resulting snow-free LAI better represents the phenology of evergreen vegetation and is intended to support studies of vegetation–snow interactions, land surface processes, and earth system modeling.

The dataset provides monthly LAI and SAI at 500 m spatial resolution globally, distributed as NetCDF-4 format files. Each file covers a 5° × 5° geographic region containing 1200 × 1200 pixels (0.00416667° or 15 arc-seconds per pixel) in the WGS84 coordinate system. The global land surface is divided into 1,447 regional tiles, with files named according to the convention RG_LatN_LonW_LatS_LonE.LSAI500m.YYYY.nc, where the latitude and longitude bounds define the tile coverage and YYYY indicates the year.

Each file contains four primary data variables: MONTHLY_LC_LAI and MONTHLY_LC_SAI representing 500 m grid LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 1200 lat × 1200 lon), and MONTHLY_PFT_LAI and MONTHLY_PFT_SAI providing PFT LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 16 PFTs × 1200 lat × 1200 lon). Grid LAI (SAI) and PFT LAI (SAI) are both available for user selection according to research demands. The grid LAI (SAI) is calculated as the area-weighted average of PFT LAI (SAI).

All LAI and SAI values are stored as unsigned byte integers with a scale factor of 0.1 and units of m2/m2, requiring multiplication by 0.1 to obtain physical values. The 16 plant functional types include various tree, shrub, grass, and crop categories ranging from tropical to boreal biomes. Coordinate variables (lat, lon, pft, mon) are included with appropriate metadata.

The snow-free Leaf Area Index (LAI) dataset is a global monthly LAI product developed for land surface and earth system modeling. It covers the period from 1985 to 2020 at 500 m spatial resolution and aims to constrain the underestimation of LAI in snow-covered regions caused by snow contamination.

The dataset was generated by integrating reprocessed MODIS Collection 6.1 LAI and GIMMS LAI4g products with plant functional type (PFT) information. Snow-affected areas were identified using satellite-based observations, and LAI was corrected at the PFT level using leaf lifespan constraints derived from the TRY plant trait database. The resulting snow-free LAI better represents the phenology of evergreen vegetation and is intended to support studies of vegetation–snow interactions, land surface processes, and earth system modeling.

The dataset provides monthly LAI and SAI at 500 m spatial resolution globally, distributed as NetCDF-4 format files. Each file covers a 5° × 5° geographic region containing 1200 × 1200 pixels (0.00416667° or 15 arc-seconds per pixel) in the WGS84 coordinate system. The global land surface is divided into 1,447 regional tiles, with files named according to the convention RG_LatN_LonW_LatS_LonE.LSAI500m.YYYY.nc, where the latitude and longitude bounds define the tile coverage and YYYY indicates the year.

Each file contains four primary data variables: MONTHLY_LC_LAI and MONTHLY_LC_SAI representing 500 m grid LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 1200 lat × 1200 lon), and MONTHLY_PFT_LAI and MONTHLY_PFT_SAI providing PFT LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 16 PFTs × 1200 lat × 1200 lon). Grid LAI (SAI) and PFT LAI (SAI) are both available for user selection according to research demands. The grid LAI (SAI) is calculated as the area-weighted average of PFT LAI (SAI).

All LAI and SAI values are stored as unsigned byte integers with a scale factor of 0.1 and units of m2/m2, requiring multiplication by 0.1 to obtain physical values. The 16 plant functional types include various tree, shrub, grass, and crop categories ranging from tropical to boreal biomes. Coordinate variables (lat, lon, pft, mon) are included with appropriate metadata.

The global land surface is divided into 1,447 regional tiles, with files named according to the convention RG_LatN_LonW_LatS_LonE.LSAI500m.YYYY.nc, where the latitude and longitude bounds define the tile coverage and YYYY indicates the year.

Each file contains four primary data variables: MONTHLY_LC_LAI and MONTHLY_LC_SAI representing 500 m grid LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 1200 lat × 1200 lon), and MONTHLY_PFT_LAI and MONTHLY_PFT_SAI providing PFT LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 16 PFTs × 1200 lat × 1200 lon). Grid LAI (SAI) and PFT LAI (SAI) are both available for user selection according to research demands. The grid LAI (SAI) is calculated as the area-weighted average of PFT LAI (SAI).

All LAI and SAI values are stored as unsigned byte integers with a scale factor of 0.1 and units of m2/m2, requiring multiplication by 0.1 to obtain physical values. The 16 plant functional types include various tree, shrub, grass, and crop categories ranging from tropical to boreal biomes. Coordinate variables (lat, lon, pft, mon) are included with appropriate metadata.

metadata.title: Derived Optimal Linear Combination Evapotranspiration - DOLCE
metadata.description:
DOLCE V3.0 is an observationally constrained hybrid Evapotranspiration (ET) dataset with uncertainty estimates. It is derived by merging four global ET datasets:

- ERA5-land (Muñoz S. J., 2019)
- FLUXCOM METEO+RS (Jung et al., 2019)
- GLEAM v3.5a and GLEAM v3.5b (Martens B. et al., 2017).

The combination of these parent datasets is based on their performance against flux tower ET, and accounts for their error dependency. The weights assigned to the parent datasets vary by seasons (Dec-May / Jun-Nov) and climate regimes based on a simplified climate regime map. DOLCE V3.0 provides time-variant estimates of its uncertainty errors. 
Similar to DOLCE V2.1, DOLCE V3.0 is monthly, has 0.25-degree spatial resolution, available over 1980 - 2018, and covers the global land.
DOLCE V3.0 is suitable for time-series and trends analysis. The reduced number of participating datasets compared to previous versions is to ensure temporal consistency throughout the covered time period.
In comparison, DOLCE V2.1, which was derived from the combination of 11 global datasets, is suitable for climatological analysis, and is less biased against flux tower observations than DOLCE V3.0. However, temporal inconsistencies around the years 2001 and 2016 were detected in DOLCE V2.1 over the tropics. These inconsistencies result from the different lengths of records of the parent datasets. We, therefore, advise the user to select an appropriate dataset for their research based on the application.

Acknowledgements
We thank Franklin (Pete) Robertson (NASA Marshall Space Flight Center) for his valuable contribution to DOLCE V3.0. 
This dataset was created by Dr Sanaa Hobeichi as part of the Centre of Excellence for Climate Extremes (CLEX) Drought research program.
references: Muñoz Sabater, J., (2019): ERA5-Land monthly averaged data from 1981 to end of 2018. Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Climate Data Store (CDS). (Accessed on 01-08-2020 ), http://doi.org/10.24381/cds.68d2bb3

Martens, B., Miralles, D.G., Lievens, H., van der Schalie, R., de Jeu, R.A.M., Fernández-Prieto, D., Beck, H.E., Dorigo, W.A., and Verhoest, N.E.C.: GLEAM v3: satellite-based land evaporation and root-zone soil moisture, Geoscientific Model Development, 10, 1903–1925,  http://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-10-1903-2017, 2017.
Jung, M., Koirala, S., Weber, U.  et al. The FLUXCOM ensemble of global land-atmosphere energy fluxes.  Sci Data   6,  74 (2019).  http://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0076-8

metadata.title: Derived Optimal Linear Combination Evapotranspiration - DOLCE
metadata.description:
Similarly to DOLCE V2.0, DOLCE V2.1 is a new hybrid Evapotranspiration (ET) dataset derived by merging 11 available global ET datasets. These include BACI, FLUXCOM RS, FLUXCOM MET, ERA5-land, GLEAM v3.3a, GLEAM v3.3b, PML-CSIRO, PSLH, MOD16, SEBS, and SRB-GEWEX.

The contribution of each dataset to DOLCE V2 is based on its ability to match field observations as well as its dependence to the other parent datasets. DOLCE V2 provides time-variant estimates of its uncertainty errors, which are consistent with its agreement with field observations.
The difference between DOLCE V2.1 and DOLCE V2.0 is that in the latter, ERA5-land was included in the merge during 2001 and 2018 only, while in the former, ERA5-land is included from 1981 to 2018.
DOLCE V2.# and its previous version DOLCE V1 use the same merging technique and provide monthly ET estimates and associated uncertainties over the global land. There are several improvements implemented in DOLCE V2.#, these include (DOLCE V2.# vs DOLCE V1):

  • Employing a wider range of parent datasets (11 parents vs 6 parent datasets)
  • Incorporating more field observations to constrain the merging technique (260 sites vs 160 sites)
  • Finer spatial resolution (0.25° vs 0.5°).
  • Longer temporal coverage (1980-2018 vs 2000-2009).


Datasets employed to derive DOLCE V2.1:

  • BACI
  • FLUXCOM RS
  • FLUXCOM MET
  • ERA5-land
  • GLEAM v3.3a
  • GLEAM v3.3b
  • PML-CSIRO
  • PSLH
  • MOD16
  • SEBS
  • SRB-GEWEX.


Field observations from flux tower networks including:

  • FLUXNET2015-tier1
  • LaThuile Free Fair Use 
  • CarboEurope
  • AmeriFlux
  • ARM
  • AsiaFlux
  • Oak Ridge
  • Ozflux

Data acquired through communication with Principal Investigators.

The final output is a monthly, 0.5-degree dataset of terrestrial Evapotranspiration and its error estimates over 1980-2018. The dataset is provided as yearly NETCDF4 files.

This dataset was produced by Dr Sanaa Hobeichi as part of her PhD thesis and of the Centre of Excellence for Climate System Science "The role of land surface forcing and feedbacks for regional climate" research program.

metadata.title: EUSFlux: Mapping Forest Carbon Uptake in the Eastern US from Upscaled Flux Tower Data
metadata.description:
This repository provides annual maps of Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) for eastern US forests at 500 m resolution, 2003–2023. NEP is predicted by a Random Forest model trained on AmeriFlux and NEON eddy covariance observations and applied to gridded MODIS, solar-induced fluorescence (GOSIF), Daymet and ERA5-Land predictors. Predictions are made for 16-day periods, gap-filled, and summed (day-weighted) to annual NEP.

From 51 candidate predictors (Table 2 of the paper), permutation importance across 100 repetitions of 5-fold spatial cross-validation retained 13; daylength was added, giving 14: forest type, NDVI, EVI, LSWI, the 30-day LSWI anomaly, NIRv, MOD09A1 surface reflectance Bands 2, 4 and 7, LAI, SIF, root-zone soil temperature, shortwave radiation and daylength. The Random Forest (100 trees, max_features = 0.33) was tuned by nested spatial cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret it.

The Zenodo repository includes:

The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests;

• An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimates at seven held-out flux tower test sites (test_sites_monthly_fluxComNEE_2003_2021.csv; column NEE_gC_m2_d1);

• The study area boundary shapefile (StudyArea.shp);

• Python scripts, Slurm job scripts and one Jupyter notebook implementing the full workflow, in four folders: input data download and checks, predictor selection and model tuning, NEP prediction and annual forest maps, and the analyses and figures of the paper (run on Indiana University’s Big Red 200 cluster; file paths must be adapted);

• Annual NEP GeoTIFFs (NEP_annual_YYYY.tif, 2003–2023) at 500 m resolution.

NEP is reported in units of gC m⁻² year⁻¹ in annual rasters, with positive values indicating net carbon uptake and negative values indicating net carbon release. Pixels outside each year’s NLCD forest mask are NoData. The sign convention follows NEP = −NEE; flux tower data and intermediate prediction rasters are in NEE convention and are sign-flipped in the analysis scripts.

A README provided within the deposit describes the contents, formats, column names, units, and provenance of all shared data files and code.

Predictor variables and benchmark data are derived from the following external datasets, which are not included in this deposit and must be obtained separately: MODIS MOD09A1, MOD13A1, MOD15A2H, MCD12Q1 and land surface temperature products (NASA LP DAAC); GOSIF SIF (University of New Hampshire); Daymet v4 (ORNL DAAC); ERA5-Land (ECMWF / Copernicus Climate Change Service); AmeriFlux/NEON flux tower observations; FLUXCOM RS+METEO (Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry); NLCD land cover (USGS), 2003–2023; forest carbon removals from Harris et al. (2021) (Global Forest Watch); and a forest stand age raster for 2010.

title: EUSFlux: Mapping Forest Carbon Uptake in the Eastern US from Upscaled Flux Tower Data

metadata.title: Compilation of hydrological datasets at the global scale
metadata.description:
Hydrological variables (evapotranspiration, precipitation, runoff, and terrestrial water storage) are distributed through several datasets that do not have the same characteristics (spatial and temporal coverage, spatial and temporal resolution). This dataset aims at providing a coherent gathering of all datasets available as of January 2021, covering at least the period from 2003 to 2014, and from 50°S to 50°N.

This file contains:

  • 14 datasets for evapotranspiration (ERA5-Land, FLUXCOM, GLDAS2.2 CLSM2.5, GLDAS2.1 CLSM2.5, GLDAS2.1 NOAH3.6, GLDAS VIC4.1.2, GLDAS2.0 CLSM2.5, GLDAS2.0 NOAH3.6, GLDAS2.0 VIC4.1.2, GLEAM, JRA55, MERRA2, MOD16, and SEBBop)
  • 11 datasets for precipitation (CPC, CRU, ERA5-Land,  PGF, GPCC, GPCP, GPM, JRA55, MERRA2, MSWEP, and TRMM)
  • 11 datasets for runoff (ERA5-Land, GLDAS2.2 CLSM2.5, GLDAS2.1 CLSM2.5, GLDAS2.1 NOAH3.6, GLDAS VIC4.1.2, GLDAS2.0 CLSM2.5, GLDAS2.0 NOAH3.6, GLDAS2.0 VIC4.1.2, GRUN, JRA55, and MERRA2)
  • 2 datasets for terrestrial water storage (GRACE CSR mascons, and GRACE JPL mascons)

Each dataset is given as the original version (on a regular grid) and also as a post-treated file averaged for 189 river basins (whose borders are also provided).

metadata.title: Data and analysis scripts for "Coupling the Noah-MP Land Surface Model to the Korean Integrated Model (KIM)"
metadata.description:
This archive contains model outputs, processed data, and analysis and plotting scripts associated with the manuscript “Coupling the Noah-MP Land Surface Model to the Korean Integrated Model (KIM).”

The archive is provided to support the reproducibility of the analyses and figures presented in the manuscript.

The archive includes output from offline land surface model simulations using the original (MPorg) and revised (MPnew) Noah-MP configurations, together with the analysis and plotting scripts used to generate the corresponding figures. KIM atmospheric model outputs used for the forecast evaluation are also provided.

Figures 13–18 were generated using the KAT (KIM Analysis/Evaluation Tools) visualization and verification system. KAT was used for remapping, calculation of verification statistics, and figure generation. KAT is not publicly available due to institutional restrictions and is therefore not included in this archive. The KIM model outputs used as input to KAT and the individual figure panels generated by KAT are provided. For Figure 19, the numerical verification data underlying the figure are also provided.

External reference datasets used in the analyses, including IFS analysis, FluxCom, GLEAM, ERA5-Land, and CERES EBAF, are not redistributed in this archive and should be obtained from their respective data providers.

Detailed information on the directory structure, datasets, software requirements, and reproduction procedures, and a summary of source-code modifications is provided in the README files included in the archive.

metadata.title: Drought risk of global terrestrial gross primary productivity in recent 40 years detected by a remote sensing-driven process model
metadata.description: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the largest flux in the global terrestrial carbon cycle and affected by multiple factors. In recent decades, drought has significantly impacted global terrestrial GPP and been projected to occur with increasing frequency and intensity. However, the drought risk of global terrestrial GPP has not been well investigated. In this study, global terrestrial GPP over the period from 1981 to 2016 was simulated with the process-based Boreal Ecosystem Productivity Simulator (BEPS) model. Then, the drought risk of terrestrial GPP was quantified as the product of frequency of drought and reduction of GPP caused by drought, which were determined using the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI). During the study period, the drought risk of terrestrial GPP exhibited detectable spatial heterogeneity, high in southeastern United States, most of South America, southern Europe, central and eastern Africa, eastern and southeastern Asia, and eastern Australia. In these regions, the maximum reduction of GPP might be above 30% in drought years relative to that in normal years. The drought risk of GPP was low at high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, in which terrestrial GPP increased slightly in drought years. The spatial pattern of the drought risk of GPP simulated by the BEPS model was close to that of FLUXCOM GPP, which was scaled from tower observations with a machine learning algorithm forced by remote sensing and meteorological data. This study advances our understanding on the impact of drought on terrestrial GPP over the globe.

metadata.title: Global Observationally-Based Land-Atmosphere Coupling Metrics (GOLAM)
metadata.description:
The Global Observationally-Based Land-Atmosphere Coupling Metrics (GOLAM) provide a comprehensive representation of land-atmosphere (L-A) coupling indices based on observationally derived (mainly satellite-based) gridded datasets. This dataset includes L-A coupling indices such as Pearson correlation coefficients and terrestrial coupling indices between daily soil moisture (SM) and surface heat fluxes, including sensible heat flux (H), evaporation (E), and evaporative fraction (EF), as well as SM memory. These indices are designed to account for random observational errors present in satellite SM measurements by employing a Markovian framework. The global patterns of surface and sub-surface SM regimes and SM-EF indicators, such as wilting point, critical SM, saturated EF, and SM-EF slope, are also quantified through segmented regression analysis. Multiple SM and flux data products are used to develop these datasets, including: two SM satellite datasets: SMAP and ESA CCI, a machine learning SM dataset: SoMo, and three surface heat flux datasets: GLEAM, CAMELE, and FluxCom-X-BASE. For consistency, the Land-Atmosphere Coupling Metrics datasets are provided at a spatial resolution of 0.25˚*0.25˚; however, the SMAP-GLEAM and SMAP-only combinations are available at both 0.1˚*0.1˚ and 0.25˚*0.25˚. The temporal coverage of these metrics depends on the input datasets and is provided across four different seasons: June-August (JJA), September-November (SON), December-February (DJF), and March-May (MAM), as well as composited warm seasons across three regions: May through September (MJJAS) for 23˚N-60˚N, November through March (NDJFM) for 23˚S-60˚S, and all months for 23˚S-23˚N. However, SM regimes are only calculated during warm seasons, depending on the latitude bands.

The source code for generating GOLAM is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17702299.

metadata.title: Impacts of Land Use Change and atmospheric CO2 on  Gross Primary Productivity (GPP), evaporation and climate in Southern Amazon (Open)
metadata.description:
This work was carried out in the scope and with the support of the project: Climate Services Through Knowledge Co-Production: A Euro-South American Initiative for Strengthening Societal Adaptation Response to Extreme Events (CLIMAX).

The project consortium includes the following institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique CNRS/Instituto Franco-Argentino sobre Estudios de Clima y sus Impactos (UMI-IFAECI) (Argentina-France); General Coordination of Earth Sciences /National Institute  for Space Research (INPE) (Brazil); Institut de Recherche pour le Développement (IRD)/ Unité Mixte de Recherche (UMR 245) (France);  Le Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l'Environnement (LSCE) (France); Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) (Germany); Technical University of Munich (TUM) (Germany) and Wageningen University and Research (WUR) Netherlands). The project is sponsored by the Collaborative Research Action (CRA) on “Climate Predictability and Inter-Regional Linkages” of the Belmont Forum, launched in 2015.

Climate variability patterns linking the South American Monsoon region, including Amazonia, with southeastern South America influence climate extremes and impact several societal sectors. More than 200 million people live in the study region, which is also one of the largest agricultural production regions of the world and home to the world’s second largest hydroelectric power plant.

The objectives of CLIMAX  include  better understanding the combined role of remote and local drivers on South American climate variability from sub-seasonal to decadal timescales, and its impact on the occurrence and intensity of extreme events. Special focus is given to an improved understanding of the effects of land use changes from the Amazon to the subtropics and their impact on climate.

  1. EXPERIMENT DESIGN

We used four models that are classified as Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) (Prentice et al., 2007; Rezende et al., 2015): Integrated Model of Land Surface Processes (INLAND) (Tourigny, 2014); Lund-Potsdam-Jena managed Land model version 4 (LPJmL4) (Schaphoff et al., 2018), Lund-Potsdam-Jena General Ecosystem Simulator (LPJ-GUESS) (Smith et al. 2001, Hickler et al., 2012), and Organising Carbon and Hydrology In Dynamic Ecosystems model (ORCHIDEE) (Krinner et al., 2005).

We used three forcings with climate data (GLDAS, GSWP3, and WATCH+WFDEI), Land Use Change (LUC) data and validation data (FLUXCOM (Remote sensor+meteorological data+artificial neural network approach), FLUXCOM (eddy covariance), MODIS (Light Use Efficiency), GLEAM, and TerraClimate (Rezende et al., 2022).

We conducted two sets of simulation experiments with different values of CO2: 1) increasing CO2 from the pre-industrial period to 2010 named historical CO2 (hist CO2); 2) constant concentration of 278 ppm of (pre-industrial) atmospheric CO2 named constant CO2 (const CO2). We ran both CO2 experiments under Land Use Change (LUC) and Potential Natural Vegetation (PNV) conditions. All combinations of CO2 and land use change resulted in four sets of simulation experiments per climate input: 1. LUC historical CO2; 2. LUC constant CO2; 3. PNV historical CO2; 4. PNV constant CO2  (Rezende et al., 2022).

2. DATA DESCRIPTION

The complete description of the data, including the climate forcing, LUC, the validation datasets, methodology, simulations, discussion and conclusion is in Rezende et al. (2022). This archive contains only the data description from the simulations (outputs) by the DGVMs.

2.1 SOFTWARE


The data were manipulated, worked, standardized, converted using the software: Climate Data Operators (cdo) version 1.7.0, Grid Analysis and Display System (Grads) (Documentation of GrADS) version 2.0.2, and RStudio Desktop version 1.3.1093 (R Core Team, 2020), through command lines and several scripts developed for this purpose. The figures were generated  with Grads, and RStudio, and some images were enhanced  with Gimp version 2.8.22. All the software used is freeware.

   2.2 PRIMARY DATA FROM SIMULATIONS

Data originating from the simulations are in monthly resolution, covering South America, with all the forcings. Despite data spanning  over 1948-2010 or 1950-2010 our study focuses on the period 1981-2010.

Variables: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) (kg m-2 month-1), evaporation  (mm month-1) and transpiration (mm month-1), and Net Primary Productivity (NPP) (kg m-2 month-1) (not used in our experiment).

The naming of the files is according to the following rules:

Example:

 2.3 SUPPLEMENTARY DATA

These interception loss data (mm month-1) were requested by a reviewer to complement the analysis and are available only for the LUC CO2 scenario and for the study region: southern Amazon (70S and 140S of latitude and 660W and 510W of longitude).

Files are named  according to the following rules:

2.4 PROCESSED DATA

Processed data cover all scenarios and input data sets and are restricted to the study area: southern Amazon (70S and 140S of latitude and 660W and 510W of longitude).They are in seasonal resolution with averages for January-February-March-April (JFMA) (rainy season) and averages for June-July-August-September (JJAS). Each of the files contains the Gross Primary Productivity variables (GPP) (kg m-2 month-1), evaporation  (mm month-1) and transpiration (mm month-1), and Net Primary Productivity (NPP) (kg m-2 month-1) (not used in our experiment).

metadata.title: Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code
metadata.description:
# Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code
 
## Overview
 
This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce the analysis of structural deficits in the conceptual rainfall-runoff model SIMHYD. The method works as follows:
 
- A differentiable version of SIMHYD carries correction slots of identical structure and capacity on eight fluxes (S1–S8).
- Forcing errors and observation errors are modeled separately from structural errors.
- A deficit is localized by comparing competing single-slot hypotheses with a significance test. The comparison uses streamflow and, where available, soil moisture, evapotranspiration (ET) and snow water equivalent (SWE).
- After localization, only the localized slots are repaired, and the repair is evaluated with variables not used in training.
 
The package covers two applications:
 
1. **Synthetic experiments.** Ten types of implanted structural deficits (D1–D9) and compound deficits (C1–C3) are tested, together with a no-deficit control (D0). Two independently generated truth sets are used (realizations r0 and r1), with eight observation combinations, two observation-quality levels and three types of input error.
2. **Application to 156 CAMELS basins** in the conterminous United States. Training uses streamflow, ESA CCI soil moisture, ERA5-Land or GLEAM evaporation, and UA SWE. Independent evaluation uses FLUXCOM-X-BASE ET and MODIS NDVI.
 
All results shown in the figures and tables of the associated article can be recomputed from the files in `data/results/`. The 12 figure scripts in `code/figs/` reproduce the article figures pixel for pixel from this package.
 
## Package structure
 
```
structural-deficit-localization/
├── README.md                 this file
├── LICENSE                   licenses of the code and the data
├── code/                     Python code (see code/README.md)
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── LICENSE               MIT License
│   ├── requirements.txt
│   ├── paths.py              locations of the data folders
│   ├── models/               differentiable SIMHYD, truth models, correction slots
│   ├── data/                 readers for CAMELS, Daymet and the gridded observation products
│   ├── synth/                generator of the synthetic truth and observations
│   ├── train/                losses and the localization model / trainer
│   ├── scripts/              experiment runners
│   ├── eval/                 analyses that produce the summary tables
│   ├── figs/                 figure scripts
│   └── tests/                unit tests
└── data/                     input data and experiment outputs (see data/README.md)
    ├── README.md
    ├── LICENSE               CC BY 4.0, with the conditions for third-party data
    ├── basins/               list of the 156 basins with their groups
    ├── camels/               CAMELS attributes, basin boundaries, basin forcing, Daymet forcing
    ├── basin_observations/   basin means of the gridded observation products
    ├── model_input/          synthetic and real data sets read by the experiments
    └── results/              outputs of all experiments and summary tables
```
 
## Quick start
 
All commands are run from the `code/` folder. The code was tested with Python 3.9 on Windows 10; the package versions are listed in `code/requirements.txt`.
 
```
cd code
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .          # 37 tests, about 3 minutes on a CPU
python -m figs.fig2_synthetic_success                # writes figures/fig2_synthetic_success.png/.pdf
```
 
The figure scripts `figs.fig1_schematic` to `figs.fig9_ndvi` and `figs.figS1_precip_prior` to `figs.figS3_phenology_maps` read only `data/` and write to a new `figures/` folder at the package root. The map figures use cartopy, which downloads the Natural Earth 1:50m boundaries on first use.
 
To rerun the experiments themselves, see `code/README.md`. The full set of experiments takes several days on a desktop computer with a 16-core CPU and one 12 GB GPU; a single experiment tag takes between about one hour and one day. A GPU is optional.
 
## Source data
 
The basin-level data in `data/` were derived from the following public data sets. Users of these data should follow the terms of use of the original providers.
 
| Data set | Use in this package | Provider and link |
|---|---|---|
| CAMELS-US time series and attributes | streamflow, forcing (P, T, PET), basin attributes, basin boundaries, Daymet basin forcing | NCAR, https://doi.org/10.5065/D6MW2F4D and https://doi.org/10.5065/D6G73C3Q |
| ESA CCI Soil Moisture v09.2 COMBINED | soil moisture observations | CEDA, https://doi.org/10.5285/d4e66299f5054129b8076fb7502949e1 |
| ERA5-Land | total evaporation and potential evaporation | Copernicus Climate Data Store, https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.e2161bac |
| GLEAM v4.3a | actual and potential evaporation | https://www.gleam.eu |
| UA SWE (NSIDC-0719) | snow water equivalent | NSIDC, https://doi.org/10.5067/0GGPB220EX6A |
| FLUXCOM-X-BASE | ET for independent evaluation | ICOS Carbon Portal, https://doi.org/10.18160/5NZG-JMJE |
| FLUXCOM RS ensemble | ET, additional comparison only | https://www.fluxcom.org |
| MOD13C1 v006 NDVI | independent evaluation of the phenology formulation | NASA LP DAAC, https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD13C1.006 |
 
The raw gridded products are not included. The scripts in `code/data/` that compute the basin means from the raw files are included; see `code/README.md`.
 
## License
 
The code in `code/` is released under the MIT License (`code/LICENSE`). The data produced in this work are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (`data/LICENSE`). These are the synthetic data sets, the experiment outputs and summaries, and the basin list. The basin-level data derived from the third-party products listed above remain subject to the terms of use of their original providers.
 
## Contact
 
Jun Guo, prof_guojun@hust.edu.cn

metadata.title: Regional datasets of long-term and coarse resolution irrigation estimates from space
metadata.description:
Description

The products are experimental datasets of long-term (approximately 20 years) Irrigation Water Use at 0.25° resolution. They cover four regions: the Contiguous United States (CONUS), the Ebro River Basin in north-eastern Spain, the Murray-Darling Basin in south-eastern Australia, and India.

These datasets are the outcome of the European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative Anthropogenic Water Use (CCI-AWU) precursor project (project link). They were produced using three different methods: SM-based (Soil-Moisture-based) Inversion, SM-based Delta, and Model-Observation Integration, which is based on the Noah-Multiparameterization model.

The SM-based Inversion method was used to produce five datasets for the four regions, each using a different SM product as input. These include ESA CCI Combined, ESA CCI Passive, ASCAT (Advanced Scatterometer), SMOS (Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity), and SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive).

The SM-based Delta method was used to produce six datasets for the four regions, each combining different SM and evapotranspiration (ET) products as input. The combinations include ESA CCI Combined SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Passive SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Active SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Combined SM & SSEBOP ET, ESA CCI Passive SM & SSEBOP ET, and ESA CCI Active SM & SSEBOP ET.

The Model-Observation Integration method was applied to the CONUS and Murray-Darling Basin regions, producing three datasets using different irrigated surface maps as input. These maps include the Landsat-Derived Global Rainfed and Irrigated-Cropland Product (referred to as "Landsat", the Relative Bias Approach (referred to as "Method1"), and the Multi-Resolution Analysis Approach (referred to as "Method2").

The irrigation products are delivered with monthly temporal aggregation.

 

Acknowledgements:

The datasets were developed as part of the ESA CCI-AWU precursor project (contract no. 4000142449/23/I-NB).

Processed datasets underlying all figures and tables of the manuscript "Quantifying the Global Impact of Forcing Variability on Hydrological and Land Surface Model Performance: A Multi-Model Evaluation". The data cover four global hydrological and land-surface models (HTESSEL, JULES, mHM, PCR-GLOBWB) driven by four precipitation forcings (EM-Earth, ERA5-Land, MSWEP, W5E5) over 1981–2019 at 0.1° resolution: precipitation differences and water-balance closure, anomaly correlation of TWSa, evapotranspiration and runoff against GravIS, FLUXCOM and GRUN, streamflow KGE at 1445 GRDC gauges, precipitation elasticity of runoff and evapotranspiration, and long-term mean discharge for the forcing-versus-model variance decomposition.

Each zip contains one analysis folder; README.md and the README_*.md files describe all variables.

The code that reads these files is archived separately (see related works).

metadata.title: RECCAP2-ocean data collection
metadata.description:
This repository contains data sets that were submitted to and analysed in the ocean branch of phase two of the REgional Carbon Cycle Assessment and Processes (RECCAP2-ocean) project.

Protocols defining the criteria for data set submissions to RECCAP2-ocean are available through the project website:
https://reccap2-ocean.github.io/protocols/

A detailed description of the submitted data sets is provided in three files contained in the supplementary.tar file. These are:

  • An overview table of all regularly submitted data sets including contact details for each submission is provided in RECCAP2-ocean_data_products_overview.xlsx.
  • The documentation of a quality control exercise is provided in QC_results_RECCAP2-ocean.pdf. All regular data sets have been quality controlled (i.e. checked for consistency with the submission protocol and general plausibility of results) by the participants of RECCAP2 (i.e. the users of the data sets).
  • A documentation of remaining data set issues that were identified after the initial quality control is provided in Remaining_data_set_issues.pdf. These remaining issues have not been corrected.

All originally submitted files were unpacked, compressed, and repacked into tar files before submission to Zenodo.

The individual submitted data sets are broadly grouped into four classes indicated by the prefix of the tar files:

  • models: Global and regional ocean biogeochemical hindcast models (GOBM/ROBM) as well as ocean data-assimilation models (data-assimilation models)
  • surface_co2: Surface ocean pCO2-observation products (pCO2 products)
  • ocean_interior: Ocean interior DIC-observation products (DIC products)
  • atmospheric _inversions: Atmospheric inversion models

Some additional files that were only used by individual chapters of RECCAP2-ocean and were not quality controlled are contained in the supplementary.tar file.

Jens Daniel Müller, RECCAP2-ocean coordinator, May 2023

on behalf of the entire RECCAP2-ocean team

metadata.title: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - Models and data sets for the ocean sink estimate in the Global Carbon Budget
metadata.description:
Global Carbon Budget Ocean - 2026 Release

This dataset provides surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs), surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products) and the ocean inverse model OCIM (interior ocean observationally-constrained estimate).

Types of files:

(1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series

(2) one file per GOBM and simulation (A, B) with gridded fields

(3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations

(4) the gridded file of the natural steady state fluxes from simulation B of six GOBMs that exclude riverine fluxes and have a globally-integrated natural steady state CO2 flux within ± 0.2 GtC yr-1. This data is used to subtract the natural steady state fluxes from the fCO2-products in regional anaylses (Figures 14 and 15)

(5) A file for the gridded CO2 fluxes and one file for the global time-series of the ocean inverse model OCIM (simulations C and B) that is used as an observationally-constrained interior ocean data-product in GCB.  

Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2026, are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 spreadsheet (https://globalcarbonbudget.org/datahub/).

The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2026 paper, the river flux adjustment needs to be added and an adjustment for the natural steady state fluxes needs to be subtracted from the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (River flux adjustment: North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2026 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes.

Three of the ten fCO2-products (UExP-FFN-U, JMA-MLR and AOML-ET) include a temperature adjustment to correct the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803).

Model simulations:

Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability)

Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability)

Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability)

Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability)

(1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly):

fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south
fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude
area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south

(2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields. Temporal resolution: monthly. Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) are saved in separate files.

fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude

(3) One file 'GCB2026_GOBMs_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc' with the globally and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs,for simulations A, B, C and D. We also report an adjusted global time-series of simulation A that accounts for model drift (Aadj). Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual.

(4) One file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_1959_2025.nc) that contains the gridded field and one file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc) that contains the global time-series of CO2 fluxes of OCIM for simulations C and B.

Further data availability:

Access and download the additional data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/

In addition to the zenodo deposit, the complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser.

In addition to the data described above, this Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release.

Model contributions and coordination:

The GCB2026-OCEAN data sets were contributed by international research groups. The creators listed in this record include the GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators and a representative of each contributing data set.

GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators: Judith Hauck and Peter Landschützer with support from Simone Le Chevère and Alizée Roobaert.

Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. 

How to cite this dataset

When using the GCB2026-OCEAN data, users should cite both of the following resources:

  1. Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the ocean carbon sink.

  2. GCB2026-OCEAN dataset: Hauck et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget Ocean - Models and data sets for the ocean sink estimate in the Global Carbon Budget [Dataset]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23723209. This dataset record provides access to the gridded model output and formally credits the participating modelling groups.

These citations are complementary and should be included when publishing analyses based on the GCB2026-OCEAN gridded model output. Users should also cite relevant individual model publications where appropriate.

Citation of these resources does not replace the GCB-OCEAN data policy, including the requirements for prior circulation of manuscripts and invitations to co-authorship where the gridded data make a significant contribution (see below and https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/)

Data use and licensing

The underlying model output is provided through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser and remains subject to the GCB-OCEAN data policy, including its acknowledgement, attribution and co-authorship requirements. Users intending to use the model output in research or publications should consult the data policy and contact the GCB-ocean coordinators and relevant modelling groups as appropriate.

The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence associated with this Zenodo record applies to the data deposited here. It does not apply to the additional gridded model output hosted externally on Wasabi, for which the GCB-OCEAN data policy governs use and redistribution.

The data policy and additional model output can be accessed through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser:

https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/

Related publication

Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data, https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2026-895

Global Carbon Budget 2026 synthesis data

The official Global Carbon Budget 2026 data supplement, including the global carbon budget spreadsheet containing aggregated ocean carbon sink estimates derived from the GOBM and fCO2-product ensembles, is available through the ICOS Carbon Portal:

https://www.icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2026

The ICOS data supplement and the GCB-OCEAN gridded model output are complementary resources. The former provides the published Global Carbon Budget synthesis results, while the latter provides access to the underlying spatially resolved ocean data.

New datasets saved as NCDF files.

Data

Post-processed TRENDYv10 DGVM data covering the period 1901-2020. Each file contains monthly/annual mean values for 19 models: CABLE-POP, CLASSIC, CLASSIC-N, CLM5.0, DLEM, IBIS, ISAM, ISBA-CTRIP, JSBACH, JULES-ES-1.1, LPJ-GUESS, LPJ, LPX-Bern, OCN, ORCHIDEE, ORCHIDEEv3, SDGVM, VISIT, YIBs. List of variables can be found at https://blogs.exeter.ac.uk/trendy/documents/ . File name: 'trendy_listofvariables_GCP2021'.

Data for three experiments (S1 - S3) is provided. For experiment details, see 'GlobalCarbonBudget-Protocol-2021-web' at https://blogs.exeter.ac.uk/trendy/documents/

Code

All data processing code is also provided. Files starting "raw#..." are run in order 1-4. Then the figure/manuscript files are executed, starting with "proc1.." - "proc3..". The remaining Figure scripts (Figures 1-5 and S1-S8) and "temp_changes.R" can be run in any order.

Any enquiries, contact Mike O'Sullivan at m.osullivan@exeter.ac.uk

metadata.title: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget
metadata.description:
TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget — 2026 Release

This dataset provides gridded terrestrial biosphere model output from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional Scale Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, contributing to the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026).

TRENDY is an international model intercomparison project that brings together simulations from dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) to investigate the global terrestrial carbon cycle and its response to environmental change, including atmospheric CO₂, climate variability and land-use change.

This release contains the final gridded model output submitted for GCB2026. The simulations support the assessment of the global land carbon sink and analyses of terrestrial carbon fluxes, stocks and their variability.

Experimental design and simulations

The TRENDY-GCB2026 protocol comprises seven simulations (S0–S6) designed to investigate the effects of changing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, nitrogen deposition, climate and land use on the terrestrial carbon cycle. Simulations S4–S6 are introduced for the first time in GCB2026.

The simulations differ in which environmental drivers vary historically and which are held at pre-industrial conditions:

Simulation CO₂ / N deposition Climate Land use / N fertilisation
S0 Fixed Fixed Fixed
S1 Transient Fixed Fixed
S2 Transient Transient Fixed
S3 Transient Transient Transient
S4 Fixed Fixed Transient
S5 Transient Fixed Transient
S6 Fixed Transient Transient

Fixed conditions correspond to pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (year 1700), repeated early 20th-century climate (1901–1920), and pre-industrial land cover, wood harvest and nitrogen inputs, as applicable. Transient conditions follow historical changes in the corresponding drivers.

Changes introduced in GCB2026

In previous Global Carbon Budgets, the land carbon sink (SLAND) was estimated primarily from S2, which assumes time-invariant pre-industrial land cover. This required a correction for sinks and sources on land subsequently converted to other uses.

For GCB2026, three additional simulations (S4–S6) allow the land sink and its attribution to environmental drivers to be calculated using simulations with transient land cover.

The land carbon sink is calculated as:

SLAND = S3 − (S4 − S0) + δL

where δL represents the transient environmental effects on land-use change emissions, estimated using bookkeeping models - and can be found at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902

The contributions from atmospheric CO₂ and nitrogen deposition and from climate are estimated as:

  • CO₂ and nitrogen deposition: S3 − S6 + δL

  • Climate: S3 − S5 + S0

These simulations provide a consistent framework for investigating terrestrial carbon fluxes under historical changes in environmental conditions and land use. Further methodological details are provided in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 Supplementary Information.

Data availability

Access and download the data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/

The complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser.

The underlying NetCDF model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. This Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release.

Model contributions and coordination

The TRENDY-GCB2026 simulations were contributed by international modelling groups. The creators listed in this record include the TRENDY coordinators and a representative of each contributing model.

TRENDY coordination: Stephen Sitch, Pierre Friedlingstein and Mike O'Sullivan.

Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata.

Release information

This dataset corresponds to TRENDY version 15, the final version of the land model simulations used for the Global Carbon Budget 2026. Please use the naming convention "TRENDY-GCB2026" in publication/presentations.

The Zenodo deposit contains the following files:

  • trendy_listofvariables_GCP2026.xlsx — definitions and specifications of model output variables.

  • TRENDY-GCB2026-manifest.csv — inventory of externally hosted gridded model output files, including filenames, paths, sizes and modification dates.

  • TRENDY-GCB2026-model-credits.csv — contributing models, model representatives and TRENDY coordinators.

  • TRENDY-GCB2026-data-policy.md — data usage, attribution and co-authorship requirements.

The underlying gridded model output is hosted on Wasabi and is accessible through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. These model output files are not deposited in Zenodo.

How to cite this dataset

When using the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output, users should cite all three of the following resources:

  1. Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the terrestrial carbon sink.

  2. TRENDY model intercomparison: Sitch et al. (2024) — This publication describes the TRENDY model intercomparison framework and its application to understanding the terrestrial carbon cycle. [https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GB008102]

  3. TRENDY-GCB2026 dataset: O'Sullivan et al. (2026) — TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget, version v15. Zenodo. [10.5281/zenodo.23561904]. This dataset record provides access to the gridded model output and formally credits the participating modelling groups.

These three citations are complementary and should be included when publishing analyses based on the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output. Users should also cite relevant individual model publications where appropriate.

Citation of these resources does not replace the TRENDY data policy, including the requirements for prior circulation of manuscripts and invitations to co-authorship where the data make a significant contribution.

Data use and licensing

The underlying model output is provided through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser and remains subject to the TRENDY data policy, including its acknowledgement, attribution and co-authorship requirements. Users intending to use the model output in research or publications should consult the data policy and contact the TRENDY coordinators and relevant modelling groups as appropriate.

The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence associated with this Zenodo record applies only to the documentation and metadata deposited on Zenodo. It does not apply to the underlying gridded model output hosted externally on Wasabi, for which the TRENDY data policy governs use and redistribution.

The TRENDY data policy and model output can be accessed through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser:

https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/

Related publication

Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data, XX, XXXX–XXXX.

[LINK]

Global Carbon Budget 2026 synthesis data

The official Global Carbon Budget 2026 data supplement, including the global carbon budget spreadsheet containing aggregated terrestrial carbon sink estimates derived from the DGVM ensemble, is available through the ICOS Carbon Portal:

https://www.icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2026

The ICOS data supplement and the TRENDY gridded model output are complementary resources. The former provides the published Global Carbon Budget synthesis results, while the latter provides access to the underlying spatially resolved terrestrial model simulations.

metadata.title: Global Carbon Budget 2023, surface ocean fugactiy of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux of individual global ocean biogechemical models and surface ocean fCO2-based data-products
metadata.description:
Surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs) and surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products).
There are three types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series, (2) one file per GOBM with gridded fields, and (3) one file with the regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs.  

Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2023 (https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-15-5301-2023), are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2023 spreadsheet.

The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 13 of the Global Carbon Budget 2023 paper (https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-15-5301-2023), the river flux adjustment needs to be added to the CO2 flux estimated from the data-products (North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2023 paper, section 2.5.1). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes.

What is in the files?

(1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly):

fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: north, tropics, south
fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude
area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south

(2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields, for simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability). Temporal resolution: monthly

fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude
area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude

(3) One file 'GCB-2023_OceanModel_RegionalBreakdown_1959-2022.nc' with the regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs, and for simulations A and B. Temporal resolution: annual.

Fair data use statement:
The data and model output provided on this site are freely available and were furnished by individual scientists who encourage their use.
Citation: Please cite the Global Carbon Budget 2023 (Friedlingstein et al., 2023, ESSD, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-15-5301-2023) for all data. In addition, please also cite the corresponding original reference for each dataset that has been used - see Table 4 in Global Carbon Budget 2023 for references of all the individual Global Ocean Biogeochemical Models and fCO2-based data-products. Further, for an overview of the Global Ocean Biogeochemical Model output, you may find it useful to cite Hauck et al. (2020, Frontiers, doi:10.3389/fmars.2020.571720).
Acknowledgement: Please add the following text in the acknowledgement of your paper: "We acknowledge the Global Carbon Project, which is responsible for the Global Carbon Budget and we thank the ocean modeling and fCO2-mapping groups for producing and making available their model and fCO2-product output."
Co-authorship: An invitation of co-authorship to the contributing groups is encouraged if these data are the central data set of the publication.

Besides the surface fCO2 and air-sea CO2 flux data that is made available open access, we make additional 3D output from the Global Ocean Biogeochemical models (GCB-ocean) available upon request and with its own data policy. Please refer to the Global Carbon Budget website for these additional data: https://globalcarbonbudgetdata.org/closed-access-requests.html

metadata.description:
The Land-Use Harmonization 2 (LUH2) dataset is updated every year for use in the annual Global Carbon Budget (GCB) simulations and publications. The LUH2-GCB2022 dataset represents the land-use data used by DGVMs and book-keeping models in the GCB 2022. It improves representation of deforestation in Brazil by using new remote sensing data from MapBiomas and it corrects previous cropland input data errors from FAO for the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

metadata.title: Land-Use Harmonization 2 for Global Carbon Budget 2025 (LUH2-GCB2025)
metadata.description:
The Land-Use Harmonization 2 (LUH2) dataset is updated every year for use in the annual Global Carbon Budget (GCB) simulations and publications. The LUH2-GCB2025 dataset represents the land-use data used by DGVMs and book-keeping models in the GCB 2025. It is extended to the current year using new input data from FAO and other sources, and extends historical trends for years without underlying input data. In particular, it incorporates new HYDE land-use data as a key input, continues to provide improved representation of deforestation in Brazil and Indonesia by using the latest versions of MapBiomas remote sensing data, and it improves cropland areas in China using data from Yu et al. 2022.

metadata.title: Impacts of Biogeochemical River Inputs on Oceanic FCO2 in MPIOM-HAMOCC
metadata.description:
Short Description: 

Impacts of biogeochemical river inputs on the spatial oceanic CO2 flux (FCO2) in the ocean biogeochemistry model HAMOCC at a 1x1° spatial resolution. The flux for each grid point is given as the difference between a preindustrial model simulation accounting for riverine inputs and another one simply compensating burial fluxes spatially (Lacroix et al., 2020). The data is used as river correction flux (Friv) in the Global Carbon Budget 2024 (Friedlingstein et al., 2025). 

References

Lacroix, F., Ilyina, T., and Hartmann, J.: Oceanic CO2 outgassing and biological production hotspots induced by pre-industrial river loads of nutrients and carbon in a global modeling approach, Biogeosciences, 17, 55–88, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-17-55-2020, 2020.
 
Friedlingstein, P., O'Sullivan, M., Jones, M. W., Andrew, R. M., Hauck, J.,  et al., : Global Carbon Budget 2024, Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 17, 965–1039, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-17-965-2025, 2025.

title: Impacts of Biogeochemical River Inputs on Oceanic FCO2 in MPIOM-HAMOCC

metadata.title: LDEO-HPD: Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory Hybrid Physics Data pCO2 Product
metadata.description:
Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory Hybrid Physics Data (LDEO-HPD)

This collection contains the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory Hybrid Physics Data (LDEO-HPD) product. This product makes near-global monthly estimates of surface ocean pCO2 from January 1982 through December 2018 with a 1ºx1º spatial resolution.  LDEO-HPD uses an eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) algorithm to make estimates of the misfit between observations and mode-based estimates. These spatiotemporal misfit estimates are then added back to the model-based estimate to make the final LDEO-HPD estimate. This is done for each of nine models part of the Global Carbon Budget 2020. 

Air-sea CO2 flux is calculated using a bulk parameterization, which is a function of wind speed. Three wind speed products are used to estimate flux. The average across these three estimates is taken as the best estimate. 

Datasets in this collection:

  • LDEO-HPD_error_v20210425_1x1_198201-201812.nc : contains estimates of the misfit from each model
  • LDEO-HPD_spco2_v20210425_1x1_198201-201812.nc : contains estimates of surface ocean pCO2 for each model
  • LDEO-HPD_fgco2_v20210425_1x1_198201-201812.nc : contains estimates of air-sea CO2 flux for each model and wind product

metadata.title: ASSESSMENT OF THE IMPACT OF ENERGY EFFICIENCY IMPROVEMENTS IN THERMAL POWER PLANTS OF UZBEKISTAN ON ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND CO₂ EMISSIONS
metadata.description: This article analyzes the impact of improving energy efficiency in thermal power plants of Uzbekistan on electricity generation volume and carbon dioxide () emissions. The study investigates the technical and economic performance indicators of thermal power plants, which constitute the main generation capacity within the country’s power system. The relationship between thermal efficiency, fuel consumption, and electricity generation was evaluated using mathematical methods. The findings demonstrate that increasing energy efficiency reduces natural gas consumption and, consequently, decreases emissions. Furthermore, the effects of modern combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) units, high-efficiency turbines, and digital control technologies on energy efficiency were assessed. The results indicate that modernizing thermal power plants in Uzbekistan plays a crucial role in strengthening energy security, ensuring the rational use of fuel resources, and reducing atmospheric greenhouse gas emissions.

metadata.description:
The Land-Use Harmonization 2 (LUH2) dataset is updated every year for use in the annual Global Carbon Budget (GCB) simulations and publications. The LUH2-GCB2026 dataset represents the land-use data used by DGVMs and book-keeping models in the GCB 2026. It is extended to the current year using new input data from FAO and other sources, and extends historical trends for years without underlying input data. In particular, it incorporates new HYDE land-use data as a key input, continues to provide improved representation of deforestation in Brazil and Indonesia by using the latest versions of MapBiomas remote sensing data, and it improves cropland areas in China using data from Yu et al. 2022. 

NOTE: Version 1.1 includes updated and corrected metadata, fill-values, missing data values, and a corrected time variable as well as an expanded list of co-authors. All other data remains the same as Version 1.

metadata.title: Gridded fossil CO2 emissions and related O2 combustion consistent with national inventories 1959-2018
metadata.description:
GCP-GridFED (version 2019.1) is a gridded fossil emissions dataset that is consistent with the national CO2 emissions reported by the Global Carbon Project (GCP). GCP-GridFEDv2019.1 provides monthly fossil CO2 emissions for the period 1959-2018 at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°. The gridded emissions estimates are provided separately for fossil CO2 emitted by the oxidation of oil, coal and natural gas, with mixed international bunker fuels considered separately, as well as for the calcination of limestone during cement production. GCP-GridFED also includes gridded uncertainties in CO2 emission, incorporating differences in uncertainty across emissions sectors and countries, and gridded estimates of corresponding O2 uptake based on oxidative ratios for oil, coal and natural gas.

GCP-GridFED was produced by scaling monthly gridded emissions for the year 2010, from the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR; version 4.3.2; Janssens-Maenhout et al., 2019), to the national annual emissions estimates compiled as part of the 2019 global carbon budget (GCB-NAE) for the years 1959-2018 (Friedlingstein et al., 2019).

The data description article is under review.

metadata.title: Land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) data for the Global Carbon Budget 2026
metadata.description:
Description

This dataset provides estimates of net land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) and their component fluxes from the three bookkeeping models used in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026): BLUE (Hansis et al., 2015), LUCE (Qin et al., 2024), and OSCAR (Gasser et al., 2020). Peat drainage emissions are from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021), and peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). The dataset further includes the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026, including estimates from national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset also includes global and gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL), which is the difference in ELUC between a simulation with transient carbon densities and a simulation with pre-industrial carbon densities. The reported net ELUC estimates already include the environmental contribution (δL).

Net ELUC and its component fluxes are available as global and national annual time series for 1850–2025. Net ELUC is also available as gridded annual time series (0.25° resolution) for 1959–2025. The data describe CO2 emissions and removals expressed as mass of carbon (C). For ELUC and its component fluxes, positive values denote emissions and negative values denote removals. The sign convention for δL is explained below. Empty cells in .xlsx files denote missing values.

The dataset contains 20 files:

  • One .xlsx file with global estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr)

  • Fourteen .xlsx files with country-level estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR, one for each of the net and component fluxes listed below (units: TgC/yr)

  • Two NetCDF files with gridded net ELUC estimates for BLUE and LUCE (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area)

  • One .xlsx file with the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr)

  • One .xlsx file with the global estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr)

  • One NetCDF file with the gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area)

Global, country-level, and gridded data

The dataset includes the following net and component fluxes. The identifiers shown in monospace are used in the corresponding country-level filenames and as worksheet names in the file with global estimates. “SC” denotes shifting cultivation, and “nonforest” refers to shrub and herbaceous vegetation:

  1. net-eluc (net ELUC): Net CO2 emissions from land-use change.

  2. clearing-allveg-total (deforestation and clearing of other vegetation (total)): Total CO2 emissions from deforestation and the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent clearing and clearing within shifting cultivation cycles.

  3. regrowth-allveg-total ((re-)growth of forest and other vegetation (total)): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of forests and shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent (re-)growth and (re-)growth within shifting cultivation cycles.

  4. wood-harvest-management (wood harvest & other management): CO2 emissions from the decay of harvested wood products and residues left on site, and CO2 removals through regrowth following harvest.

  5. cropland-pasture-urban (cropland-pasture-urban transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between cropland, pasture, and urban areas.

  6. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): CO2 emissions from peat drainage and anthropogenic peat fires. Peat drainage emissions are the average of estimates from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021). Peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025).

  7. clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation.

  8. clearing-forest-sc (deforestation in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from deforestation within shifting cultivation cycles.

  9. clearing-nonforest-permanent (permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 emissions from the permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation.

  10. clearing-nonforest-sc (clearing of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles.

  11. regrowth-forest-permanent (permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation): CO2 removals through forest growth and regrowth following permanent afforestation and reforestation.

  12. regrowth-forest-sc (forest (re-)growth in SC cycles): CO2 removals through forest regrowth within shifting cultivation cycles.

  13. regrowth-nonforest-permanent (permanent (re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation following permanent land-use changes.

  14. regrowth-nonforest-sc ((re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 removals through the regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles.

Components 2–6 sum to net ELUC (component 1). Components 7–10 are subdivisions of component 2 and sum to its total. Components 11–14 are subdivisions of component 3 and sum to its total.

Environmental contribution to ELUC (δL)

The environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) is defined as the difference in ELUC between simulations using transient and pre-industrial carbon densities (transient minus pre-industrial). Positive values indicate higher ELUC under transient carbon densities, and negative values indicate lower ELUC.

Annual estimates are provided for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR in two files:

  • GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_global_1850-2025.xlsx: Global estimates for 1850–2025 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr).
  • GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_gridded_1959-2025.nc: Gridded estimates for 1959–2025 (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area).

For OSCAR, country-level estimates were spatially disaggregated to a 0.25° grid using the spatial patterns of gross emissions and gross removals from BLUE (see Supplementary Section S.2.2 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)).

Data underlying Figure 8

The file GCB2026_Figure8_Data.xlsx contains the datasets used in Figure 8 (a-c) of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr), within the period 1990–2025 for bookkeeping estimates and the sink in managed forests and for the period 2000–2025 for national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs; 2024 data replicated in 2025) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset groups and variables are as follows:

Bookkeeping models (BMs) and peat datasets

  • net-eluc (net ELUC): Component 1 in the above list.

  • clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): Component 7 in the above list.

  • other-transitions (other transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between shrubland, herbaceous vegetation, cropland, pasture, and urban areas, corresponding to the sum of components 5, 9, 10, 13, and 14 in the list above.

  • forest (fluxes on forest land): CO2 fluxes on forest land, including permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation, net CO2 fluxes from shifting cultivation in forests, and net CO2 fluxes from wood harvest & other management, corresponding to the sum of components 4, 8, 11, and 12 in the above list.

  • peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): Component 6 in the above list.

National greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs)

Inventory estimates are from Melo et al. (2026).

  • net-lulucf-flux (net LULUCF flux): Net CO2 fluxes from land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF).

  • clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation.

  • peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires). Emissions from drainage of organic soils and fires on organic soils.

  • other-transitions (other non-forest land uses): Net CO2 fluxes from cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements, and other land, including land remaining in these categories and transitions between them. Emissions from organic soils are reported under peat-emissions.

  • forest (fluxes on forest land): Net CO2 fluxes from forest land remaining forest land and land converted to forest land, including harvested wood products and excluding organic soils.

Dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs)

  • managed-forest-sink: The CO2 sink in managed forests estimated by DGVMs (see Supplementary Sections S.2.4 and S.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)).

Atmospheric inversions

  • net-lulucf-flux: The net LULUCF flux estimated by atmospheric inversions (see Supplementary Section S.2.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)).

Citation and data policy

When using this dataset, please cite the specific dataset version used and the accompanying Global Carbon Budget 2026 publication:

  • Schwingshackl, C., Gasser, T., Qin, Z., Seeberg, G., Fu, Z., and Pongratz, J. (2026). Land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) data for the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (Version 1.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902

  • Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data Discussions [preprint]. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2026-895

For analyses using individual model estimates or the additional datasets underlying Figure 8, we also recommend citing the relevant references listed below.

Gridded data for the individual ELUC component fluxes are available from the authors upon request. For studies using gridded data, the contributing modellers should be offered the opportunity to participate early in the research process. Potential co-authorship should be discussed at that stage, taking into account the role of the data in the study and the modellers’ contributions.

References

Conchedda, G., and Tubiello, F. N. (2020). Drainage of organic soils and GHG emissions: validation with country data. Earth System Science Data, 12, 3113–3137. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-12-3113-2020
